Photograph: Mark Cocker Country diary Trees and forests Country diary: Autumn’s great colour display is a matter of life and death
 Buxton, Derbyshire: The golden hue of birch trees is underrated, yet this is a process of stress, as deciduous trees prepare for next spring
 Mark Cocker Tue 17 Nov 2026 00.30 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Best time of the year, this!” said the man walking by as I was photographing the autumn birches at Hogshaw nature reserve . I was tempted to add “Amen”.
 What’s so compelling about these trees is their impasto swatch of colour, which looks so powerful this morning. Naming it, however, is trickier. It changes with the light and perhaps with your own mood, but it’s somewhere between the brilliant lemon of new life and the darker sepia of life lost.
 Surely this is the essence of autumn itself: a mix of life and death, a perpetual duality so memorably captured by Edward Thomas in his poem The Thrush , where he writes “I must remember / What died into April / And consider what will be born / Of a fair November.” What’s born for me this fair November is the following reflection: birches have underrated leaves because they are small and lack the reds present in sycamore or horse chestnut leaves, but at their best they have a wonderfully ambiguous golden hue.
 View image in fullscreen Freshly fallen birch leaves at Hogshaw nature reserve, with one small deceiver (fungi) middle left. Photograph: Mark Cocker We should recall further that all deciduous-leaf colour change is driven by the trees seeking to prevent loss of precious resources. Chlorophyll – the origin of April’s greenness – is costly to produce. So, as the days shorten, trees break down their chloroplasts and store them for next year. That process brings stress, and renders them vulnerable to DNA-destroying free radicals. To neutralise this threat, trees produce antioxidants called anthocyanins. It’s these that turn leaves those wonderful red tones.
 The requirement to drop foliage and store away chlorophyll, which operates at a cellular level within each tree – each leaf, even – is actually cosmic in origins. For the Earth, travelling at 100,000km an hour with a tilt of 23.4 degrees, deprives all trees in one whole planetary hemisphere of the conditions to sustain their full respiratory processes. Trees therefore adjust to the cyclical pattern, during which they will travel – as will you, of course – 940 million km every year. So, what you see when you look at a birch leaf’s gold is our planet’s journey around the sun.
